newsitem.title: USA: Paccar sees DAF deal adding to earnings.
newsitem.headline: Paccar sees DAF deal adding to earnings.

text.p: Paccar Inc Vice Chairman Mike Tembreull said Monday he expected the company's planned acquisition of DAF Trucks NV of the Netherlands to be accretive to its earnings immediately.
"We don't anticipate any restructuring costs or any charges of any kind," Tembreull said in a conference call with analysts monitored by Reuters.

He also said that despite the move into Europe, Paccar still saw room to grow in its core North American market. The company aimed to raise its share of U.S. and Canadian heavy-duty truck sales to 25 percent from 21 percent, he said.
"We do see great opportunities in Europe," Tembreull said. "But we also see growth in the United States and Canada."
He said the European market is about the same size as the U.S. market, but European sales are expected to fall by 5 to 10 percent next year.
Tembreull said Paccar planned to finance the friendly acquisition, still subject to shareholder approval, through a combination of cash and debt.
"We have all this cash, and we're anticipating a better return than we've been able to receive on that," he said.
Paccar had $184 million in cash at the end of last year.
Tembreull said the acquisition of DAF includes $50 million in debt, but he said the company's balance sheet includes cash in excess of that amount. He said the debt cannot be prepaid.

The transaction requires approval of 80 percent of the shareholders of privately held DAF, Tembreull said. The Dutch government is the largest shareholder with a 39 percent stake, followed by Belgium with 10 percent. Institutional investors hold the rest.
He said DAF had about a 20 percent share of the British truck market, 30 percent of the Dutch market and 15 percent of the Belgian market, as well as a presence in several other countries.

"The company is profitable right now, and it is interested in expanding and growing its market share in all of these different countries," Tembreull said. "We see this as another Kenworth or Peterbilt, which will help Paccar achieve its profit goals in the future." He was referring to Paccar's existing Kenworth and Peterbilt truck lines.
He said DAF's cost structure was among the lowest in Europe because of favorable work rules negotiated in the predecessor company's 1993 bankruptcy.
In Britain and Israel, where the two companies now compete, Paccar will allow the brands to continue to go head to head, Tembreull said.
Tembreull also said Paccar would look closely at the possibility of expanding DAF's profitable parts business, which includes engines.
